auto.text: A match breakdown shows a two-ball auto in a quarterfinal at the first Israel district event, beside 1690's five-ball.
A recap describes a five-ball auto in the first Einstein final, with four scored in the upper hub.

cycle.text: Cargo passes a color sensor; a wheel spins out to throw the wrong color out the back or in to send the right one up the conveyor. With two in, the Limelight gives angle and distance to the hub and a formula gives the shooter's angle and speed.

endgame.text: The driver touches the rung with the telescopes; they close, hand over to static arms, angle back, open past the next rung, angle in until motor current rises, and close. The team gives 10 seconds to traversal.

fallback.text: In the second Einstein final, a recap commentator says, it spun out of good defense many times to reach the launch pad area for its shots.

changed.text: Side pieces on the intake were removed because two balls could enter the dribbler together and get stuck.
The video's host says the team missed a few shots at its first event and was accurate by the third Israel event and the championship.

outcome.text: 66-12-0 in official play; won the Turing division, championship finalist; captain of the Turing alliance on Einstein; ranked 5 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 65.95, Turing).

facts.text: Swerve, as a team member mentions
A commenter lists it among swerve robots with a fixed shooter

solves.text: Collect cargo from every side with as much surface contact as possible

facts.text: Works like a dribbler, with flat belt and poly cords
Chosen to suit other subassemblies, the swerve drivetrain among them (garbled captions)
The team color comes from the field system

Incoming cargo touches the intake's back roller and a black wheel; that wheel spins out to eject it, past the roller and an orange wheel above, out the back, or in toward a wall of churros and the conveyor
One infrared sensor shows when an ejected cargo has left, another when a kept cargo is in place

solves.text: Shoot from many places around the field

facts.text: Static arcs, cut on the team's own CNC, mesh with similar arcs on a moving hood
A main wheel and back wheels mitigate spin
A Limelight gives angle and distance to the hub
Preferred spot is around the edge of the tarmac and a bit further

cost.text: A recap of the Einstein finals says two cargo shot up against the hub under defense bounced into each other and one or both missed; in the second and third it shot almost only from the launch pad area

functions.name: Climber

solves.text: Climb rung to rung in a sensor-driven sequence

functions.type: tilting telescopic arms with static arms

facts.text: Bumper switches on the static arms show contact with the bar
Springs tilt the telescopes to a 3D printed mechanical stop as a winch gives rope; the rope pulls them back
Motor current shows when the telescopes meet the next rung
Climb to traversal by the team's account, about
A 1 g zip tie between two gears of the climber arm brakes it; reversing the motor drops the tie, and the software backup never had to run in competition
A commenter names it among simple climbers without pneumatics

decisions.choice: Aim for the middle of the hub, near the back side
decisions.because: it lowers the chance of cargo bouncing upward

decisions.choice: No side pieces on the intake
decisions.because: two balls could go into the dribbler together and get stuck
